https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgmk.text: Figure caption, Watch: What we know about Tupac murder suspect Duane "Keffe D" Davis By Anoushka Mutanda-Dougherty Â and Â Shaimaa Khalil ,Â Los Angeles Correspondent Published 8 hours ago It's been three decades filled with mystery, conspiracies - and anger. The drive-by shooting that killed rap superstar Tupac Shakur on 7 September 1996 changed the trajectory of hip-hop and elevated the rapper from the face of the genre to a cultural icon. His killing became one of popular culture's great mysteries, with countless theories but no arrests until 2023, when Duane "Keffe D" Davis was unexpectedly charged with murdering the famous rapper. The 63-year-old former gang boss is due to stand trial in Las Vegas, where he is accused of murder with a deadly weapon with the intent to promote, further or assist a criminal gang. He's pleaded not guilty. If convicted, he faces life in prison without parole. The trial is likely to unravel the intricacies of the bitter and deadly East Coast vs West Coast rap rivalries and turf wars between the Bloods and the Crips street gangs that were immortalised in rap lyrics and news reports in the 1990s. It could also include several celebrity witnesses - including Suge Knight, the former CEO of Death Row Records, who has been thought of as the last surviving witness to Shakur's death. But the complicated case hinges almost exclusively on one key piece of evidence: a book co-authored by Davis that he has argued is partially a piece of fiction. Jury selection in the case began on Monday, with opening arguments due to start on 17 August. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Tupac's murder helped elevate the rapper from the face of gangsta rap to a cultural icon To understand how the case became so mythologised, you have to go back to rivalries that grew larger than the men at its centre. In the Los Angeles gang landscape of the 1990s, there was a vicious turf war between the Bloods, often represented by the colour red, and Crips, who often wore blue. But that territorial dispute spread through the airwaves as part of a bigger national rivalry - East Coast v West Coast rap. The genre dispute was represented by two rival record companies that defined 1990s hip-hop: Knight's Death Row Records and Sean "Diddy" Combs' Bad Boy Records. "The funny thing about it is Tupac is actually an East Coast rapper," said Jeff Pearlman, author of Only God Can Judge Me: The Many Lives of Tupac Shakur. Born in New York City, Tupac moved to northern California as a teenager. He became known as a southern California rapper after signing with Death Row Records, which included acts like Snoop Dogg and Dr Dre. Santi Elijah Holley, author of An Amerikan Family: The Shakurs and the Nation They Created, says the Death Row persona never told the whole story. Tupac's mother Afeni was a Black Panther and he grew up around the black liberation movement. Holley says his music became his politics: "His activism was his art, his lyrics." He acted in a number of Hollywood movies, and released hip-hop's first double album, All Eyez on Me, which sold over 5,000,000 copies. That album, which debuted months before his death, cemented his place in the cannon of gangsta rap, a genre that celebrated the violent life of street criminals and drug dealers. After he was shot in Las Vegas on 7 September 1996, he became immortalised as a kind of martyr for the lifestyle he helped make famous. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Duane Davis, who's accused of orchestrating Tupac's murder, was the uncle of Orlando Anderson, an alleged member of the South Side Compton Crips That fatal night began when Tupac and Knight attended a boxing match between Mike Tyson and Bruce Seldon at the MGM Grand. After the match, surveillance footage captured Tupac and members of his entourage, who police have said were associated the Mob Piru Bloods street gang, attacking a man named Orlando Anderson, an alleged member of the South Side Compton Crips. About three hours after the attack, Tupac was riding in the passenger seat of Knight's BMW driving through Las Vegas when a white Cadillac pulled alongside them and opened fire. Tupac was hit four times and died six days later. For nearly three decades, the killing remained one of America's most famous unsolved murders. There is no single explanation why. Las Vegas police have long said witnesses refused to co-operate. Members of Tupac's entourage said police initially treated them like suspects and failed to follow important leads. Within weeks of the shooting, investigators had identified Anderson from the MGM footage and questioned him. He denied involvement and was never charged; he was killed in an unrelated shooting in 1998. Over the years, police say they pursued thousands of tips, but the case stalled amid disappearing witnesses, many of whom were also killed in gang-related shootings, limited physical evidence, and a street code that forbade co-operation with police. It was years later when Anderson's uncle, Davis, started talking and according to police, blew the case wide open again. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Tupac and Snoop Dogg were both part of the LA record label Death Row Records, run by Suge Knight It was ultimately the death of another legendary rapper that helped unravel Tupac's shooting death. Months after Shakur was gunned down, Biggie Smalls, or the Notorious BIG, was killed in a drive-by shooting in Los Angeles. Both rappers were the stars of their respective rival record labels - Shakur with Death Row Records and Biggie with Bad Boy Records. Biggie's case has remained unsolved, with no arrests or suspects. In the mid 2000s the Los Angeles Police Department reopened the investigation and spoke with Davis, who was at a party with Biggie before the fatal shooting. While Davis said he didn't have information about Biggie's death, he did have knowledge of Tupac's case and shared that he was in the car when the rapper was shot and killed. He told police the information in exchange that he not be charged. That deal stuck until years later, when Davis went public with his knowledge. He co-authored a memoir in 2019 titled Compton Street Legend, that claimed he not only was inside the vehicle when Tupac was shot, but he was also the person who "tossed" the gun used to kill him into the backseat of the Cadillac. He never claimed to be the person who opened fire. Davis also elaborated on the shooting to the media, detailing information to reporters in interviews. Las Vegas police said his public statements had "reinvigorated" the investigation. Over the next couple of years they spent time corroborating Davis' account and then in 2023, searched his home and seized multiple computers, two tubs of photographs and a slew of Tupac-related material, including a Vibe magazine. He was arrested later that year. Prosecutors have alleged that Tupac's killing was in retaliation for the beating of Davis' nephew - Orlando Anderson - just hours before the shooting. They claim that Davis was the architect of the crime, who ordered the shooting and supplied the deadly weapon to further gang criminal conduct. Listen to Fame Under Fire: The Tupac Murder Trial Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Months after Shakur was gunned down, Biggie Smalls or the Notorious BIG, was killed in a drive-by shooting Nevada prosecutors argued that by publicly talking about what happened on the night of Tupac's death and writing a book where he claimed to have supplied the gun, Davis had broken the agreement he entered into with law enforcement. A judge later sided with the prosecutor's argument, opening the door for Davis' arrest. Davis and his defence team have argued that the book was co-authored and sections were embellished or fictionalised to make a profit, and they should not be viewed as direct admissions. In an interview last week with a local TV news station, Davis denied being in Las Vegas when Tupac was killed and distanced himself from the memoir that lists him as an author. "I did not write that book," Davis told Fox 5. "A ghost writer wrote that." He also said he might take the stand and testify at his trial. "If I have to, I will." Trial attorney Shaun Kent told the BBC: "This is what makes this case so fascinating. The two biggest pieces of evidence against Keffe D came from Keffe D. "Keffe D has the right to take the stand and say 'I made all this up. I lied to sell copies of the book. I lied to the police. I'm a liar but I did not murder Tupac.'" Davis has also publicly stated multiple times that Bad Boy Records head Sean "Diddy" Combs had offered him $1m to kill Death Row Records rivals Tupac and Knight. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Tupac is now one of the most recogniseable faces in hip hop Combs is currently serving a 50-month prison sentence after being convicted for two counts of transportation for the purposes of prostitution in New York. He has repeatedly denied allegations that he was involved in Tupac's death. Prosecutors have released a list of potential witnesses who could be called to testify, with over 200 names, including members of Tupac's family, former mayor of Las Vegas Oscar Goodman and former Los Angeles police Detective Greg Kading. Prosecutors have also named Knight, although it's unclear if the rap impresario will testify, as he's previously said he would not. "This would be huge as he has never offered law enforcement any information that would lead to the conviction of anyone," Kent said. "This trial is going to be a legal scholar's Super Bowl." https://www.politico.eu/article/germany-.text: EU capitals must be able to intervene to stop new legislation from Brussels if they say it’s too burdensome for governments and businesses, the leaders of Germany, Italy and Belgium wrote on Monday. In a letter addressed to European Council President António Costa and seen by POLITICO, the three leaders said the bloc needs an “emergency brake” mechanism to help boost its flagging economic competitiveness. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Belgian Prime Minister Bart de Wever also called to “significantly accelerate planning and approval procedures,” suspend “certain regulatory areas for a specified period” under a new “priority rule.” Advertisement Advertisement “We call for further ambitious simplification packages to decisively advance the cutting of red tape in the European Union,” they wrote, adding that the Commission must ease the burden “first and foremost” on small and medium-sized businesses. “More broadly,” the letter reads, “our common objective should be to prevent unnecessary regulatory burdens and related costs from causing permanent losses of European industrial capacity and further weakening investment and competitiveness.” Coming days before an EU leaders’ meeting, the call echoes demands first stated in March after a summit focused on European competitiveness, and it comes amid worsening signs for the bloc’s industrial sector. Leaders will debate the EU’s long-term budget, energy prices, and support for Ukraine when they gather in Brussels on Thursday for a two-day European Council summit.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner was leading plans for the development in Belgrade, which had attracted protests – the banner reads: ‘We won’t give up the General Staff building.’ Photograph: Andrej Isaković/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner was leading plans for the development in Belgrade, which had attracted protests – the banner reads: ‘We won’t give up the General Staff building.’ Photograph: Andrej Isaković/AFP/Getty Images Serbia Serbian prosecutor who investigated Belgrade Trump tower project ‘targeted with spyware’ Apparent attempt to hack Rade Bajić’s iPhone comes amid efforts to undermine landmark criminal case Tom Burgis Tue 20 Oct 2026 05.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 05.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Serbian prosecutor who investigated the authorities’ allegedly illegal scheme to help the Trumps build a tower in Belgrade has been targeted with advanced spyware, expert analysis indicates. Revealed: Serbian ruler’s secret role in ‘illegal’ effort to help Trump business Read more The finding suggests a disturbing new element in the authoritarian Serbian regime’s campaign to undermine what is believed to be the first criminal case related to global moneymaking drive of the US president’s family, which critics describe as a “pay to play” scheme trading the Trump administration’s favour for business opportunities. Rade Bajić, the targeted prosecutor, said: “In my opinion, my involvement in this case was the sole reason for this unlawful spyware attack.” Analysts at the Citizen Lab, a digital forensics laboratory, have not so far established who was behind the attack but the Serbian regime has previously been caught using spyware against its opponents. View image in fullscreen A screenshot from Trumpbelgrade.com shows the renderings of the proposed Belgrade development. Photograph: Trumpbelgrade.com News of the alleged hack follows the Guardian’s revelations last week that Aleksandar Vučić, Serbia’s president, personally ordered that a cherished site in Belgrade be stripped of its legal protection so it could be handed over for a $500m Trump hotel and tower. Vučić, one of the Balkans’ most influential nationalists, hosted the US president’s son Donald Jr – “dear Don” , as he calls him – and son-in-law Jared Kushner as he ingratiated himself with the Trumps. At the weekend, Vučić responded to the Guardian’s revelations about his role in the scandal by confirming details of a previously secret meeting. He indicated he had done nothing wrong. “I fought for my people,” he said. “And that’s what I’ll continue to do in the future.” Last year prosecutors brought a landmark indictment against senior members of Vučić’s regime, accusing them of abusing their office to unlawfully strip the General Staff building – a monument to Serbia’s recent difficult history – of its protected status. They face years in jail if convicted. Kushner, who was leading the Trump Belgrade development, called off the plans after the charges were made public. Vučić vowed reprisals , denouncing the prosecutors, including Bajić, a member of the specialised organised-crime unit that brought the indictment. Bajić has said he was taken off the case without explanation shortly before the indictment was published. He went on to address one of the rolling protests against the regime triggered by widespread corruption, telling demonstrators in February: “The law will be equal for all.” View image in fullscreen Jared Kushner, left, was hosted in Belgrade by the then president, Aleksandar Vučić. Photograph: Instagram/Aleksandar Vucic In August, Bajić received a message from Apple saying it had “detected a targeted mercenary attack against your iPhone”. Citizen Lab researchers, who have been analysing Bajić’s phone, said this was “ a high confidence indicator that his device was likely targeted with mercenary spyware, such as Pegasus”. Working with the Share Foundation, a Serbian rights group, they previously identified spyware attacks against anti-government protesters. In at least one case, the Citizen Lab analysts discovered Pegasus on a protester’s phone. “A zero-click infection with Pegasus spyware would not have been visible to the target, and would give the Pegasus attacker total access to the device,” they said of that discovery. The Guardian’s Pegasus Project revealed how journalists, activists, politicians and others have been targeted by governments using the spyware. NSO Group, the Israel-based company that makes Pegasus, has been approached for comment. View image in fullscreen Aleksander Vučić, seen here with Donald Trump Jr, right, cannot run for a third presidential term so is attempting to become Serbia’s prime minister. Photograph: Facebook/Aleksandar Vucic Vučić, who stepped down late last month and called snap elections for 25 October, hoping to prolong his 12-year rule by switching from president to prime minister. He has been approached for comment, as has the prosecutors’ unit, which has said it may bring more charges in the General Staff building case. Representatives of the Trumps and Kushner have denied they engaged in “pay to play” arrangements and said they were not involved in the Serbian authorities’ decision to strip the building of its protected status. https://gq.co.za/wealth/2026-10-08-cogni.text: GET THE LATEST ISSUE OF GQ Cognitive Debt: How AI is changing your brain Cognitive Debt: How AI is changing your brain Image: J Studios Ask someone to quote a sentence from the email they just sent. If they drafted it with artificial intelligence, chances are their brain will go blank. This isn't just wishful thinking: in the MIT Media Lab's Your Brain on ChatGPT experiment, 83% of students who wrote an essay with the chatbot's help couldn't correctly reproduce a single sentence of their own text minutes after submitting it. Among those who wrote it entirely on their own, the lapse was almost negligible. The researchers gave it a name that sounds like a bank: cognitive debt. It works like any quick loan. Today you save yourself the effort; tomorrow you pay back interest in memory, judgment, and style. For four months, the team used electroencephalography to measure the brain activity of 54 Boston university students divided into three groups, and connectivity between brain regions decreased in direct proportion to external assistance: highest in those who typed manually, intermediate with Google, and lowest with ChatGPT. It's wise to read the fine print before throwing your laptop out the window. The sample size is tiny, EEG doesn't detect what's happening in the brain's deeper layers, and other major studies on the topic (a Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon survey of 319 professionals, another of 666 people in the UK) find correlations, not causality. No one has yet photographed a brain that has shrunk due to a chatbot. What does emerge, study after study, is a pattern of behavior. One that is recognizable long before it appears on any scan. Symptoms that something is changing in your brain 1. Author's amnesia. You reread something you signed on Tuesday and it sounds like someone else's writing, like a report from a colleague you never really liked. Psychology has explained this since 1978, when Norman Slamecka and Peter Graf described the generation effect: we remember what we produce much better than what we simply read. When the machine generates, your brain stops being an author and becomes a reader, and readers forget . In the MIT study, the ChatGPT group was also the one that felt the least ownership of the essay; those who wrote it without help spoke of it with something akin to pride. 2. The Tab Reflection. You haven't even finished formulating your question and you already have the chat open. For an email subject line, for the name of that actor from The Sopranos , for calculating a tip. Michael Gerlich, from SBS Swiss Business School, found a clear negative correlation in 666 people between the frequent use of AI tools and scores in critical thinking, with cognitive offloading acting as a bridge between the two. The pattern was most pronounced among 17- to 25-year-olds. The phenomenon has precedents: in 2011, a study published in Science dubbed the Google effect , that tendency to remember where a piece of information is rather than the information itself. The difference is one of degree. Google returned ten links that you had to read, compare, and discard; the chatbot serves you the conclusion already spoon-fed. 3. Blind faith in the well-written paragraph. You check less. You notice it when you forward a summary without having opened the original document or when you accept a figure because it was well-written. The Microsoft Research and Carnegie Mellon survey of 319 knowledge workers puts it with unsettling precision: the more trust you place in AI, the less critical effort you apply ; the more self-confidence, the more you apply. Respondents skipped verification primarily in tasks they considered secondary and in those they didn't master enough to judge the response. The problem is that AI writes with the self-assurance of a radio pundit at 7 a.m., and self-assurance is easily mistaken for truth. 4. You no longer see the mistake. This is the most serious and best-documented symptom. In Poland, 19 veteran endoscopists (each with over 2,000 colonoscopies) began working with an AI system that flags polyps in real time. When, months later, they returned to examining without the tool, their adenoma detection rate had dropped from 28.4% to 22.4%, according to a 2025 article in The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology. A clinical eye, literally. In January 2026 came the most troubling statistic, given its source: Anthropic, the company that makes the Claude assistant, published a controlled trial in which programmers who learned a new library with AI help scored 50% on the subsequent exam, compared to 67% for those who programmed by hand. The biggest difference was in debugging. In other words, the skill that suffers first is precisely the one needed to monitor the machine. 5. Your prose sounds like everyone else's. The essays from the ChatGPT group at MIT sounded suspiciously similar, and a Microsoft survey detected the same phenomenon in office work: less diversity of results for the same task. You'll recognize it in yourself when you start listing everything in threes, ending paragraphs with "in short," and constructing sentences with the "it's not just this, it's that" template. Your voice used to be a collection of quirks, favorite words, and graceful errors. The machine smooths them out, leaving them at a passable, perfectly forgettable average. 6. The writer's block becomes unbearable. The blank page has always been daunting; now, it's also exhausting. Thinking without assistance begins to resemble climbing stairs in a broken elevator. In the fourth session of the MIT experiment , researchers removed ChatGPT from those who had used it from the beginning, and their brains continued to function at half speed: less connectivity, worse recall of what they had written. The debt was still there even after the lender had left. Conversely, those who had written on their own and received the tool at the end showed high brain activity. That detail, often lost in the headlines, is the best news of the study and the basis for everything that follows. Training to help you recover your brain The brain behaves like any muscle : what isn't used, is lost. The advantage is that it also responds like a muscle, and the cognitive debt is repaid. The key lies in the order of operations suggested by MIT itself: think first, delegate later. No one is asking you to uninstall anything. Simply use AI like you would a gym machine, with proper technique and understanding what each exercise targets. The ten-minute ink challenge (against author amnesia). Before opening the chat, spend ten minutes writing your version of the issue: the thesis, three key ideas, the order. By hand, if possible. Only then ask for help to polish, complete, or refute it. This is the sequence used by the group at MIT who transitioned from writing alone to using ChatGPT and kept their brains active. The final text will be a hybrid, but the skeleton will be yours, and the skeleton is what you remember. The exit exam (against amnesia and blind faith). Every time you close an AI-generated task, close the tab as well and write from memory, in five lines, what the text says and why. If you can't do it, you haven't understood it: you've only memorized it. The technique is called retrieval practice and is one of the most solid findings in the psychology of learning . In 2006, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke proved that recalling what has been learned consolidates the memory much better than rereading it. Fifteen minutes of writer's block (to combat the tab reflex and intolerance of being stuck). When your mind goes blank, set a timer and forbid yourself from chatting until it goes off. Walk, doodle, talk to yourself. Robert Bjork, a psychologist at UCLA, has spent decades advocating for desirable difficulties: the effort of retrieving or resolving something that resists is precisely what consolidates it. The frustration of those fifteen minutes is the exercise, not a side effect. AI as a sparring partner, not a black sheep (against blind faith). Change the verb in your requests. Instead of “write to me,” try “ask me three questions I haven’t asked myself,” “rebut my argument,” or “explain why this works.” The Anthropic study found that the problem wasn’t using AI, but how: those who delegated everything to it or tasked it with fixing every mistake scored below 40% on the exam, while those who asked it conceptual questions or requested explanations scored between 65% and 86%. The day without a safety net and the hunt for errors (against blindness to error). Set aside one task a week, something you're good at, to complete entirely without assistance, just like a pilot who continues to land manually even though the plane can do it on its own. And every time the AI ​​gives you something important, force yourself to find at least one mistake, an inaccuracy, or a piece of information that you need to verify with the original source. If you don't find any, look harder: your goal is to keep alive the keen eye that Polish endoscopists lost in a matter of months. Long reading sessions and stolen phrases (against average prose). Thirty minutes a day of reading on paper, without notifications, from authors with recognizable voices. Underline and copy by hand a phrase from someone else that you would have liked to have written yourself. Neuroscientist Maryanne Wolf, author of Reader, Come Home , argues that deep reading is a skill the brain builds and that dismantles if it isn't practiced. Your own voice is nourished by digested voices of others; the statistical average of all of them nourishes no one. The body also thinks (for all of the above). Aerobic exercise is probably the best-studied tool for protecting the brain. In a 2011 study by Kirk Erickson, a year of brisk walking three times a week increased the volume of the hippocampus, the key structure for memory, by about 2%. Add to that a weekly walk without GPS in an area you only vaguely know. London taxi drivers, forced to memorize thousands of streets, develop a larger-than-average posterior hippocampus, according to the work of Eleanor Maguire. Navigating on your own is the oldest version of this same exercise. And get enough sleep: it's during sleep that the brain decides what to store. Try the initial test on yourself. Find something you typed this week—an email, a report, a difficult message—and try to quote a sentence without looking. If you can quote it completely, including the commas, you're up to date. If not, you know where to start paying it off. The sentence you know by heart is often the only one that truly belongs to you. https://science20.com/robert_walker/how_.text: Space How A "Dwarf Planet" Gas Giant Could Challenge IAU Definition - Pluto, Ceres, Haumea Etc Can All Be Planets By Robert Walker in Robert Inventor March 13, 2017 Opens in a new window Opens in a new window Opens in a new window Ethan Siegel has just written an article, "The Science Has Spoken: Pluto Will Never Be A Planet Again", so this is a response to it. I'll argue that far from "story over", actually we could make a discovery tomorrow that would turn the whole thing on its head and make their definition untenable. This will become particularly acute if we ever find a gas giant in the outer reaches of our solar system, too far away to clear its orbit. And we could find such a planet. Ethan Siegel has just written an article, "The Science Has Spoken: Pluto Will Never Be A Planet Again" , so this is a response to it. I'll argue that far from "story over", actually we could make a discovery tomorrow that would turn the whole thing on its head and make their definition untenable. This will become particularly acute if we ever find a gas giant in the outer reaches of our solar system, too far away to clear its orbit. And we could find such a planet. The WISE survey only ruled out Saturn sized planets out to 10,000 AU and Jupiter sized ones out to 26,000 au . We could have gas giants that orbit our sun over 1.5 light years away, or over 100,000 au. For consistency, we would have to call it a "Gas Giant Dwarf Planet Non Planet". To explain why, first, here is the graph from his article which he uses to show the neat division between large planets that clear their neighbourhood and small ones that don't. But I've extended it to a light year, and let's use Alan Stern's terminology - let's call an orbit clearing planet an "uber planet" and one that doesn't, an "unter planet": The vertical axis shows its mass in Earth masses. Full size image here . The three lines here show three possible definitions for the IAU planet, or uber planet. As he points out, there's a clear division between the IAU planets, or "uber planets" as I will call them in this article and the unter planets. The unter planets are all much smaller, and what's more, there are no objects that are anywhere close to the line between the two. That’s kind of neat for as long as this pattern holds, that all unter planets are much smaller than uber planets. I think it’s already a bit strange to say they are not planets, when they are “dwarf planets”. But there’s more than that. The diagram already shows that an Earth sized object could be a dwarf planet and not a planet if it was far away as 700 au, the predicted semi-major axis for "Planet Nine" if it exists. Now, it's true that they predict it to be Neptune sized, and at that mass, 17 times the mass of Earth, it would sneak in as a planet. But one hypothesis is that "Planet 9" is not one planet but several planets in resonance, which according to some Spanish astronomers may explain the observations better. Here are the two competing definitions: The IAU's original, 2006 definition: It needs to be in hydrostatic equilibrium, or have enough gravity to pull it into an ellipsoidal shape. It needs to orbit the Sun and not any other body. And it needs to clear its orbit of any planetesimals or planetary competitors. The planetary scientist's proposed geophysical definition for a planet: A planet is a sub-stellar mass body that has never undergone nuclear fusion and that has sufficient self-gravitation to assume a spheroidal shape adequately described by a triaxial ellipsoid regardless of its orbital parameter. I have just one issue with this proposal the requirement of a triaxial spheroidal shape. All the dwarf planets and planets we know of so far are approximately spheres, oblates spheres, or triaxial ellipsoids (all of which can be described as triaxial spheroids with one or more axis the same length). But that's not necessarily going to continue to be true. Artist's impression of Haumea spinning. It has this rugby ball shape, not because of tidal effects of its moons, but because it spins so fast. The mathematician Jacobi predicted back in 1834 that sufficiently rapidly spinning planets would e"break symmetry" and become triaxial spheriods instead of oblate spheriods. As it spins faster, other shapes become the preferred shape: A rapidly spinning planet eventually becomes a dual lobed "Roche world" then finally three, and then four lobes become favoured, and a sufficiently rapidly spinning planet, just on the verge of breaking apart, is stable as a torus, with a hole in the middle, like a doughnut. For more on this see my So You Thought You Knew What Spinning Planets Look Like? ... A double planet, even a non contact binary, with the two planets close together, will no longer be a triaxial spheriod, but more egg shaped, due to the tidal effects. If you say that the planet has to be self gravitating and in hydrostatic equilibrium, then the details of the shape don't matter.
